**How to use Worksheet A (the “Capital Expense Worksheet”) to figure the medical‑expense portion of a home improvement** Worksheet A is designed to tell you how much of the cost of a home‑improvement that was done for a disability can be treated as a medical expense. Follow the steps in the order shown on the worksheet. Keep a copy for your records. | Step | What you do | Why you do it | |------|-------------|---------------| | **1.** | **Enter the amount you paid for the home improvement** (the total cash you spent). | This is the “gross” cost of the project. | | **2.** | **Enter the value of your home **immediately after** the improvement.** | This is the market value of the house once the work is finished. | | **3.** | **Enter the value of your home **immediately before** the improvement.** | This is the market value of the house before any work was done. | | **4.** | **Subtract line 3 from line 2**. The result is the **increase in home value** that the improvement created. | This tells you how much of the cost actually added to the property’s worth. | | **5.** | **Compare line 4 to line 1**:
‑ If line 4 ≥ line 1 → **No medical expense** (the improvement’s value is equal to or greater than what you paid). Stop here.
‑ If line 4 < line 1 → **Proceed to the next section**. | When the added value is less than what you spent, the “excess” portion may be deductible as a medical expense. | | **6.** | **Enter the reimbursement you received from your employer’s policy** (if any). | Reimbursements reduce the amount you actually paid out‑of‑pocket. | | **7.** | **Enter the reimbursement you received from your own (personal) policy** (if any). | Same purpose as step 6. | | **8.** | **Add lines 6 and 7**. This is the **total reimbursement** you received. | Gives the total amount that was paid back to you. | | **9.** | **Divide line 1 (your out‑of‑pocket cost) by line 8 (total reimbursement).** | This yields the **percentage of the cost that was not reimbursed** (i.e., the portion you actually paid). | | **10.** | **Enter the total medical expenses you paid during the year** (including the home‑improvement cost and any other qualified medical expenses). | The IRS limits the deduction to the amount of medical expenses that exceed a threshold (7.5 % or 10 % of AGI). | | **11.** | **If the amount on line 10 is at least as much as the amount on line 8, stop** – there is **no excess reimbursement** to include as income. | When your total medical expenses already exceed the reimbursement, the whole unreimbursed portion can be deducted. | | **12.** | **Multiply line 9 (the unreimbursed‑percentage) by line 10 (total medical expenses).** This gives the **portion of your total medical expenses that is attributable to the unreimbursed part of the home improvement**. | This isolates the deductible amount that comes from the home‑improvement. | | **13.** | **Subtract the result of step 12 from line 1**. The result is the **amount of the home‑improvement cost that you can claim as a medical expense**. | This is the final deductible amount for the improvement. | | **14.** | **Enter employer’s contribution to the annual cost of the employer’s policy** (the amount your employer pays toward the policy). | Needed for the next calculation if you have to report excess reimbursement as income. | | **15.** | **Enter the total annual cost of the employer’s policy** (the full premium). | | | **16.** | **Divide line 14 by line 15**. The result is the **percentage of the policy’s cost that is your employer’s contribution**. | This percentage tells you how much of any excess reimbursement must be reported as “other income” on your Form 1040. | ### Putting it together – a quick example | Item | Amount | |------|--------| | Cost of improvement (line 1) | $12,000 | | Home value after (line 2) | $250,000 | | Home value before (line 3) | $240,000 | | Increase in value (line 4) | $10,000 (‑ $12,000 < $10,000 → go on) | | Employer reimbursement (line 6) | $2,000 | | Personal policy reimbursement (line 7) | $1,000 | | Total reimbursement (line 8) | $3,000 | | Unreimbursed % (line 9) | $12,000 ÷ $3,000 = 4 → 100 % (you paid all of it) | | Total medical expenses for the year (line 10) | $8,000 | | Portion attributable to improvement (line 12) | 100 % × $8,000 = $8,000 | | Deductible home‑improvement expense (line 13) | $12,000 – $8,000 = $4,000 | In this example you could claim **$4,000** of the home‑improvement cost as a medical expense on Schedule A. --- ### Bottom line 1. **Determine how much of the improvement added value to the home** (lines 1‑4). 2. **If the added value is less than what you paid, calculate the unreimbursed portion** (lines 6‑9). 3. **Apply the unreimbursed percentage to your total medical expenses** to isolate the deductible amount (lines 10‑13). 4. **The result on line 13 is the amount you may include as a medical expense** for the home improvement. Keep the completed Worksheet A with your tax records; the IRS may ask to see how you arrived at the deductible figure.
reference: Worksheet A is the capital expense worksheet you use to figure the amount of your capital expense to include in your medical expenses for a home improvement, and you should keep it for your records.

The Taxpayer Advocate Service (TAS) does not issue its own set of rules for figuring the amount of excess medical‑expense reimbursement that must be reported on Form 1040 or Form 1040‑SR.  In the material provided the TAS is mentioned only as a resource for help (the two web‑site links for contacting the service), and all of the actual calculation guidance comes from the IRS worksheets that are part of Publication 502.

**What the guidance says (IRS, not TAS):**

1. **If you have only one health‑insurance policy** – use **Worksheet B**.  
   *Enter the amount your employer contributed, the total annual cost of the policy, divide the contribution by the cost, multiply that fraction by the amount of excess reimbursement, and report the result as “other income” on Form 1040/1040‑SR.*

2. **If you have more than one policy** – use **Worksheet C**.  
   *Enter the reimbursements from the employer‑paid policy and from your own policy, work through the steps that allocate the excess reimbursement between the policies, then apply the percentage of the employer’s contribution (from the employer‑contribution/total‑cost ratio) to the excess amount.  The final figure is the amount you must include as other income on Form 1040/1040‑SR.*

3. **Reimbursements received in a later year** – report the reimbursement as income up to the amount you previously deducted as a medical expense (see Pub. 525, “Recoveries”).

4. **Reimbursements for expenses you never deducted** – do not include the reimbursement in income up to the amount of the expense; only any amount that exceeds the expense is potentially taxable.

**How to report it:**  
The amount calculated with the appropriate worksheet is entered on the “Other income” line of Form 1040 or Form 1040‑SR (the line number varies by year, but it is the line designated for “Other income” on the main 1040 page).

**What TAS says:**  
The Taxpayer Advocate Service’s role is to help taxpayers understand and apply these IRS rules, not to provide a separate formula.  If you need assistance applying the worksheets or determining the correct amount to report, the TAS can be contacted through the URLs listed in the publication, but the actual calculation must follow the IRS worksheets described above.
reference: The Taxpayer Advocate Service (TAS) is an independent organization within the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) that helps taxpayers resolve problems with the IRS and understand their rights. According to the guidance referenced in the context, when you receive an insurance reimbursement for medical expenses that you previously deducted, you must calculate the excess reimbursement by multiplying line 7 by line 10. The resulting amount is the total excess reimbursement you must report as other income on Form 1040 or Form 1040‑SR. If the reimbursement is received in a later year, you generally report it as income up to the amount you previously deducted as medical expenses, but you do not report any portion that exceeds the unreduced medical deductions from the earlier year. For detailed rules on recoveries of previously claimed itemized deductions, see Pub. 525.

**Interaction of cost‑of‑capital and the dividend‑surplus rule**

* When MSTR evaluates a new preferred‑stock issuance it looks at the **all‑in cost** of the transaction – the cash that will have to be paid as preferred‑stock dividends plus any dilution that results from issuing additional equity or using cash from the USD Reserve.  
* Those dividend cash‑flows are a **fixed short‑term expense** (the company even calls them “relatively fixed” in the expense‑budget discussion).  Because the company must fund them, the cost‑of‑capital analysis is run together with the **dividend‑eligibility test** required by Delaware law: a dividend can be declared only if the corporation has (i) **surplus** (assets – liabilities – statutory capital) **or** (ii) net profits for the current or immediately‑preceding fiscal year, and (iii) “legally available” funds so that the payment does not render the company insolvent.  

In practice this means that:

1. **The higher the preferred‑stock dividend rate (or the more variable the rate, as with STRC or STRF), the larger the cash outlay that must be covered by the company’s surplus or earnings.**  
2. **If the all‑in cost of the offering (including the dividend obligation) would exhaust the surplus or exceed the net profit that can be legally used, the company would either have to raise additional equity/debt, refinance existing indebtedness, or decide not to pay the dividend.**  
3. Consequently, the cost‑of‑capital assessment is not just a financing decision; it is also a test of whether the company will be able to meet the statutory dividend‑payment condition after the offering is completed.

**Role of deferred taxes**

* The discussion of “profitability and expectations for future profitability” notes that **deferred‑tax balances and the valuation allowance on deferred‑tax assets affect net income** in the period when the allowance is adjusted.  
* Because the dividend‑surplus rule looks at **net profits** (or surplus) and because “legally available” funds must be measured after all liabilities—including deferred‑tax liabilities—are taken into account, any change in the **deferred‑tax asset valuation allowance** can increase or decrease the reported net profit and the amount of surplus that is available for dividends.  
* Therefore, when MSTR assesses its ability to declare a preferred‑stock dividend, it must consider not only cash on hand and earnings from operations, but also **how deferred‑tax adjustments will impact the net profit figure and the overall surplus** that underpins the legal right to pay dividends.

**In short:**  
The cost‑of‑capital analysis for a preferred‑stock offering forces MSTR to quantify the cash needed for future dividend payments, and that cash must be supported by legally available surplus or net profit. Deferred‑tax accounting directly influences the net‑profit and surplus calculations, so any change in deferred‑tax assets or allowances can materially affect whether the company meets the Delaware requirement to declare and pay those dividends.

When deciding whether a dividend can actually be paid, the company must also verify that it has either surplus – defined as total assets less liabilities and statutory capital – or, if surplus is insufficient, net profits from the current or immediately preceding fiscal year (as explained in <2‑hop>). In addition, Delaware law requires that the funds be “legally available” so that the dividend does not render the corporation insolvent. The IRS’s on‑line assistance utilities can be used to work out whether a cooperative corporation meets the “at least 80 % of gross income paid by tenant‑stock‑holders” test.

* **Tax Withholding Estimator (W‑4 app)** – lets you enter all of the corporation’s (or your personal) wages, dividends, rents and other income and see the total amount of taxable income that will be reported. By comparing that total to the amount you know is paid to the tenant‑stock‑holders you can quickly see whether the 80 % floor is met.

* **Earned Income Tax Credit Assistant** – helps you determine whether the income you receive as a tenant‑stock‑holder qualifies as earned income, which is the portion that counts toward the 80 % threshold.

* **Interactive Tax Assistant (ITA)** – includes searchable topics on cooperative housing and “tenant‑stock‑holder” rules, so you can get specific guidance on how the IRS treats the corporation’s gross income and what documentation you must keep.

* **Online EIN Application** – provides the corporation with a proper employer‑identification number, which is required when you report the corporation’s gross receipts and the amounts paid to tenant‑stock‑holders on the tax return.

* **Forms and Publications (IRS.gov/Forms)** – give you the worksheets and schedules (e.g., Schedule K‑1, Form 1120‑C) needed to break out the corporation’s total gross income and the portion attributable to tenant‑stock‑holders, making the 80 % calculation transparent.

By using these tools you can:

1. **Calculate the corporation’s total gross income** for the year.  
2. **Identify the portion paid to tenant‑stock‑holders** (through wages, dividends, rent‑share, etc.).  
3. **Compare the two figures** to confirm that the tenant‑stock‑holder share is ≥ 80 %.  

Thus, the IRS’s web‑based calculators, assistants, and form resources give you the data‑entry, guidance and worksheets needed to verify that the tenant‑stock‑holder income threshold is satisfied.

- The credit applies to **qualified residential clean‑energy property**, which includes **solar electric (photovoltaic) systems**, solar water‑heating, fuel‑cell, small‑wind, geothermal‑heat‑pump, and **battery‑storage** equipment.  
- The 30 % rate is the same for every year in the 2022‑2025 window; there is **no lifetime dollar limit** on the credit, but the credit **expires after 2025**.  
- If a new building or a major reconstruction is placed in service **after 2025**, the residential clean‑energy credit **cannot be claimed**, even if the solar electric system itself was installed earlier.

**How the solar‑electric credit interacts with the energy‑efficient home‑improvement credit**

1. **Separate credits for different types of property**  
   * **Residential clean‑energy credit** – for *energy‑producing* systems (solar electric, solar thermal, wind, fuel‑cell, geothermal, battery storage).  
   * **Energy‑efficient home‑improvement credit** (the renamed non‑business energy property credit) – for *energy‑saving* improvements such as qualified windows, skylights, exterior doors, heat‑pump systems, heat‑pump water heaters, biomass stoves/boilers, etc.

2. **Both credits are available for property placed in service through 2025**  
   - The home‑improvement credit also expires after 2025 (no credit for property placed in service on or after January 1 2026).  
   - Because the credits cover different categories, a homeowner can claim **both** in the same tax year **provided the expenditures qualify under the separate rules** (e.g., a solar PV system gets the 30 % clean‑energy credit, while new ENERGY‑STAR windows get the home‑improvement credit).

3. **No double‑dipping**  
   - The same expense cannot be used for both credits. If an item is classified as a “qualified energy‑producing property” (solar electric), it is only eligible for the residential clean‑energy credit.  
   - Conversely, a window or door that improves efficiency but does not generate energy is only eligible for the home‑improvement credit.

4. **Documentation**  
   - For the clean‑energy credit, keep receipts, manufacturer’s certification, and proof that the system was placed in service by 12/31/2025.  
   - For the home‑improvement credit (effective 2025), a four‑character alphanumeric **Qualified Manufacturer Identification Number (QMID)** must be listed for each qualifying item.

**Bottom line**

- **Qualified solar‑electric installations** placed in service **anytime from 2022 through December 31 2025** qualify for a **30 % credit** on the cost of the system (including installation).  
- The credit **ends after 2025**; any solar‑electric system placed in service in 2026 or later is not eligible.  
- This credit is **independent** of the **energy‑efficient home‑improvement credit**, which covers different, non‑producing efficiency upgrades and also expires after 2025. Homeowners can claim both credits in the same year as long as each expense meets the specific eligibility criteria for its respective credit.

Consequently, solar electric installations placed in service during the 2006‑2025 period qualify for the credit. This credit is distinct from the earlier credit for home energy improvements (1977‑1987) and from the credit for qualified energy‑efficiency home improvements (2006‑2007, 2009‑2025).

According to the IRS guidance, a farmer or fisher who receives pension or annuity payments outside the United States can **elect not to have tax withheld** if the following steps are taken:

1. **Be a U.S. citizen or resident alien** – the election is only available to people who are U.S. citizens or resident aliens.  

2. **Give the payer your own home address that is located in the United States or in a U.S. territory** – the address must be **your personal residence**, not the address of a nominee, trustee, or agent.  

3. **Provide that address to the payer before the payment is made** – the election must be made before the income is paid or credited, so the payer knows to treat the distribution as “non‑withheld.”  

When the payer receives a genuine U.S. (or U.S.‑territory) home address for the beneficiary, the payer is allowed to **skip the 30 % (or treaty‑reduced) withholding** that would otherwise apply to benefits delivered abroad. If the address supplied is only for a nominee or agent and not the beneficiary’s own home address, the payer must still withhold tax.  

In short, the farmer or fisher avoids withholding by **informing the payer of their own U.S.‑territory home address** (and confirming their U.S. citizen or resident status) before the pension or annuity is paid.

**BGCs (Biosynthetic Gene Clusters)** are tightly packed groups of genes that together encode the enzymes required to synthesize a particular secondary‑metabolite (SM).  
Typical members of a BGC include genes for polyketide synthases (PKSs), non‑ribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs), terpene synthases and various tailoring enzymes. Because the genes are co‑located and co‑regulated, the whole pathway for producing a specific natural product is organized in a single chromosomal region.

**Why BGCs matter**

1. **Source of bioactive natural products** – The metabolites produced from BGCs (polyketides, non‑ribosomal peptides, terpenes, etc.) often have potent biological activities such as antimicrobial, anticancer, or immunomodulatory effects. These compounds are valuable leads for drug discovery and pharmaceutical development.

2. **Hidden chemical diversity** – Many BGCs are silent or poorly expressed under standard laboratory conditions. Unlocking them (by epigenetic modifiers, co‑cultivation, precursor feeding, ribosomal engineering, etc.) can reveal novel chemicals that are not otherwise accessible.

3. **Predictable genome‑mining targets** – Because BGCs contain conserved signature genes (e.g., PKS, NRPS domains), bioinformatic tools such as AntiSMASH, rBAN, and other genome‑mining pipelines can locate and annotate them in sequenced genomes. This enables systematic exploration of the metabolic potential of microbes without needing to culture every strain.

4. **Biotechnological and agricultural relevance** – Activation of BGCs can improve production of useful metabolites (e.g., fungal antibiotics, pigments, virulence factors) and can be harnessed to enhance plant resistance, produce industrial enzymes, or generate novel agro‑chemicals.

5. **Evolutionary insight** – BGCs illustrate how secondary‑metabolism pathways evolve as coordinated gene blocks, allowing rapid acquisition or loss of entire biosynthetic capabilities.

In short, BGCs are the genetic “blueprints” for making secondary metabolites, and they matter because they are the key to discovering, producing, and engineering the chemically diverse, biologically active compounds that underpin many therapeutic, agricultural, and industrial applications.

**Summary**

Anabaena’s edible nature, ability to survive the shrimp gut, ease of genetic engineering, and exceptionally high photosynthetic/biomass productivity make it an attractive chassis for delivering oral vaccines. The VP28‑expressing Anabaena sp. PCC 7210 demonstrated:

* Very high VP28 transcription (≈2 × 10⁵ DNA copies mL⁻¹) and protein output (≈34 mg L⁻¹),
* A dramatic improvement in shrimp survival (68 % vs <21 % for all non‑transgenic controls),
* And a massive boost in photosynthetic activity (≈25–43‑fold over wild‑type).

These results collectively show that the transgenic Anabaena strain is both a potent antigen producer and a highly efficient, sustainable delivery vehicle for oral vaccination against WSSV in shrimp.

The pharmacokinetic experiment showed that **bSS was detectable in the brain 24 h after an intraperitoneal injection**, proving that the molecule can cross the blood‑brain barrier in vivo. **What ACENPs do**

- **Nanoparticle type** – ACENPs are exosome‑like nanoparticles isolated from the medicinal plant *Acorus calamus* (ACENPs = Acorus calamus‑derived exosome‑like nanoparticles).  
- **Size & dose** – They are ~122 nm in diameter and are active at particle concentrations up to 2 × 10¹⁰ particles mL⁻¹.  
- **Biological effect** – When breast‑cancer cells are exposed to ACENPs their viability drops (≈ 17 %–36 % reduction depending on the cell line) and the cells undergo programmed cell death.  

**How ACENPs get into breast‑cancer cells**

1. **Efficient internalisation** – Fluorescence microscopy of Nile‑Red‑labelled ACENPs shows rapid uptake by all three breast‑cancer lines tested (ER⁺ MCF‑7, HER2⁺ MDA‑MB‑453, and triple‑negative MDA‑MB‑231).  
2. **Likely uptake route** – The discussion cites similar plant‑derived vesicles that enter MDA‑MB‑231 cells via a caveolin‑1‑dependent endocytic pathway; inhibition of caveolin‑1 markedly reduces uptake. By analogy, ACENPs are thought to be internalised through caveolae‑mediated endocytosis (or other clathrin‑independent mechanisms) that are highly expressed on these cancer cells.  

**How ACENPs trigger caspase‑dependent apoptosis**

1. **Delivery of bioactive cargo** – Metabolomic profiling shows ACENPs contain several anticancer metabolites (α‑asarone, venlafaxine, 10‑hydroxy‑2‑decenoic acid, trigonelline, gingerol, etc.). These molecules are released inside the cell after uptake.  
2. **Modulation of apoptotic regulators** – After treatment, Western‑blot and gene‑expression analyses reveal:  
   - ↑ Bax (pro‑apoptotic)  
   - ↓ Bcl‑2 (anti‑apoptotic)  
3. **Caspase cascade activation** – The same studies (and prior reports on α‑asarone) demonstrate up‑regulation of caspase‑3, ‑8 and ‑9 activities, indicating that the intrinsic (mitochondrial) and extrinsic pathways converge on caspase activation.  
4. **Morphological confirmation** – AO/EB staining, DAPI nuclear fragmentation, and Annexin V‑FITC/PI flow cytometry all show classic apoptotic features (membrane blebbing, chromatin condensation, phosphatidylserine externalisation).  

**Summary**

ACENPs are plant‑derived, ~120 nm exosome‑like vesicles that are readily taken up by breast‑cancer cells—most likely via caveolin‑1‑mediated endocytosis. Inside the cells they release anticancer phytochemicals that shift the Bax/Bcl‑2 balance toward apoptosis, activate the caspase‑3/8/9 cascade, and consequently induce caspase‑dependent programmed cell death, leading to a measurable loss of cell viability.
reference: The A. calamus‑derived exosome‑like nanoparticles (ACENPs) are taken up efficiently by several breast cancer cell lines, including MCF‑7, MDA‑MB‑453 and MDA‑MB‑231, as shown by the first‑time internalization experiments. Once inside the cells, ACENPs modulate the Bax/Bcl‑2 ratio by up‑regulating the pro‑apoptotic protein Bax and down‑regulating the anti‑apoptotic protein Bcl‑2. This shift leads to mitochondrial outer‑membrane permeabilization, release of cytochrome c into the cytosol, and activation of the caspase cascade, resulting in caspase‑dependent apoptosis. The exact uptake mechanism is not fully defined, but related studies on Perilla‑leaf‑derived extracellular vesicles suggest that high caveolin‑1 expression on MDA‑MB‑231 cells facilitates internalization, and inhibition of caveolin‑1 reduces uptake, implying a possible similar pathway for ACENPs.

**Checking a mortgage‑interest refund**

1. **Look at the Form 1098 you receive from your lender.**  
   * If the lender refunded any mortgage‑interest you had previously deducted, the amount will appear in **Box 4** of the Form 1098.  
   * The refund amount shown in Box 4 is the “refund status” – it tells you that a refund was issued and how much it was for.  

2. **Report the refund on your return.**  
   * The refund is generally **taxable** and must be included in income for the year you receive it (see Pub. 525, “Recoveries”).  

3. **If you haven’t received a Form 1098 or you can’t find the box‑4 amount,** call the mortgage holder and ask them to send you the statement that shows any refund of over‑paid interest.

---

**Deducting mortgage points**

1. **Get the points information from your lender’s Form 1098.**  
   * The Form 1098 lists the **deductible points** you paid during the year.  

2. **Enter the points on Schedule A (Form 1040).**  
   * **Line 8c** – “Points” (if you have a Form 1098).  
   * If you did **not** receive a Form 1098, put the deductible points on **Line 8b** (interest) and **Line 8c** (points) as appropriate.

3. **Amortization rule (the usual case).**  
   * Points are treated as prepaid interest and must be **deducted over the life of the mortgage** (the number of years of the loan).  

4. **Exceptions that let you deduct the full amount in the year paid:**  
   * Points paid **at settlement** when you buy a home.  
   * Points **paid by the seller** on your behalf (the seller’s payment is treated as if you paid them).  
   * Points on a home purchased **between Jan 1 1991 and Apr 3 1994** that you elected to deduct in the year paid.  
   * Points on a home bought **after Apr 3 1994** (you may deduct them in the year of purchase if they meet the “points” definition).  

5. **If you didn’t deduct the points earlier:**  
   * You may claim them on the tax year in which the home is sold, provided they have not already been deducted (see Pub. 936, “Home Mortgage Interest Deduction”).  

6. **When the mortgage ends early** (prepayment, refinance, foreclosure, etc.), any **remaining undeducted points** can be taken in that year, unless you refinance with the same lender—in which case the points must continue to be amortized over the new loan term.

---

**In short**

* Check Box 4 of your Form 1098 (or ask the lender) to see whether a mortgage‑interest refund was made and include that amount as taxable income.  
* Use the points amount shown on the same Form 1098 (or calculate it yourself) and report it on Schedule A, line 8c, following the amortization rules or the specific exceptions that allow a full‑year deduction.

**Costs**

* **Direct breach‑related costs** – money spent to investigate the incident, contain it, remediate the vulnerability, notify users and regulators, and rebuild or replace affected systems.  
* **Legal‑defence and settlement costs** – expenses of defending class‑action suits, mass‑arbitration demands and other privacy‑related litigation, plus any settlements, judgments or adverse litigation‑related expenses.  
* **Regulatory fines and penalties** – monetary sanctions that can run to €20 million or 4 % of global annual revenue (whichever is higher) and other civil or criminal penalties that may be imposed by U.S., EU or other jurisdictions.  
* **Operational and compliance costs** – additional staff, technology and process investments required to meet GDPR, U.S. state privacy statutes, the ePrivacy Directive, the DMA/DSA, FTC consent orders, youth‑social‑media rules, etc.; costs of modifying data‑handling practices, adding new controls, or terminating relationships with vendors that cannot meet the new rules.  
* **Business‑impact costs** – loss of advertising revenue, refunds or concessions to advertisers, higher fees paid to third‑party content or distribution partners, and the indirect cost of reputational damage that can drive away users, marketers and partners.  
* **Share‑based compensation and other expense items** – any acquisition‑related share‑based compensation that must be recorded as a result of the breach or the regulatory response.

**Regulatory consequences**

* **Government enforcement actions** – investigations, audits, inspections, consent‑decrees, orders to cease or modify data‑processing activities, bans on processing personal data, and even criminal liability for company officials.  
* **Litigation exposure** – class‑action lawsuits, mass‑arbitration demands and private‑right‑of‑action claims that can seek statutory damages on a per‑violation basis, potentially resulting in “monumental” damages depending on the volume of data and number of violations.  
* **Additional reporting and oversight** – heightened reporting requirements, ongoing regulatory monitoring, and the possibility of being placed under continuous supervisory regimes.  
* **Restrictions on advertising products** – limits on the ability to target or serve ads, changes to product design, or removal of certain ad‑related features in jurisdictions where privacy or content‑moderation laws become more restrictive.  
* **Potential market limitations** – the need to terminate or redesign relationships with foreign vendors, customers or partners that cannot meet new privacy standards, which can shrink market opportunities and increase costs.  

In short, privacy breaches and the evolving privacy‑related legislative landscape expose Meta’s ad business to **substantial remediation, legal and compliance expenditures, large fines and penalties, and revenue‑impacting operational changes**, while also creating **significant regulatory risk through investigations, enforcement actions, litigation and mandatory changes to how its advertising services are delivered**.

The company’s liquidity strategy is built around three complementary pillars – a very large pool of cash‑like assets, a flexible revolving credit facility, and disciplined credit‑risk controls – that together allow it to fund the growing cash outflows tied to its operating‑lease commitments while keeping credit‑risk exposure low.

**1.  Cash‑and‑short‑term‑investment buffer that covers lease cash‑flows**  
* **Size of the buffer** – As of the most recent reporting dates the firm held roughly $95 billion of cash, cash equivalents and short‑term, investment‑grade fixed‑income securities (e.g., $94.6 bn at June 30 2025).  This pool is far larger than the operating‑lease cash payments reported for the three years ($6.1 bn in 2023, $7.4 bn in 2024 and $9.1 bn in 2025).  
* **Liquidity focus** – The short‑term investments are deliberately “highly liquid, investment‑grade” and diversified, so they can be converted to cash quickly to meet lease‑related outflows or any other short‑term need.  
* **Operating cash generation** – The company also expects cash generated from operations to continue to be “sufficient to fund our operating activities and cash commitments for investing and financing activities … for at least the next twelve months and thereafter for the foreseeable future.”  The operating‑lease cash outflows are therefore covered first by cash on hand, then by cash flow from operations, and finally by the credit facility if needed.

**2.  Revolving credit facility as a back‑stop**  
* **Facility terms** – A revolving line of credit with JPMorgan Chase (and other lenders) matures in September 2030, bears a variable base rate plus a margin, and carries commitment fees on any unused portion.  
* **Covenant discipline** – The company is in compliance with all financial covenants (e.g., a minimum fixed‑charge coverage ratio of 1.25‑1.00 and a net‑leverage ratio ≤ 4.0‑1.00).  Maintaining compliance preserves the facility and prevents a default that could cut off this source of liquidity.  
* **Availability** – Although the exact amount available at year‑end 2025 is redacted, the facility is described as “sufficient to meet our anticipated operating cash needs for at least the next twelve months.”  It therefore acts as a safety net for any timing mismatch between lease payments and cash inflows.

**3.  Credit‑risk mitigation and concentration management**  
* **High‑quality custodians** – Cash and cash equivalents are kept at “high‑credit‑quality financial institutions,” even when balances exceed FDIC‑insured limits.  The firm continuously monitors the financial condition of these banks.  
* **Customer‑receivable diversification** – No single customer accounts for more than 10 % of accounts receivable or revenue, limiting concentration risk.  The company regularly reviews the creditworthiness of its online‑marketplace partners and brand‑partner customers, and it can require advance payments when a counter‑party’s credit profile deteriorates.  
* **Ongoing monitoring** – The firm conducts “ongoing evaluations of customers and brand partners’ financial conditions” and has policies to “require advance payment to mitigate potential credit risks.”  This proactive stance reduces the chance that a large receivable default would impair liquidity.  

**Putting it together**

When lease‑related cash outflows rise (from $6.1 bn in 2023 to $9.1 bn in 2025), the company first draws on its massive cash and short‑term‑investment balances, which are already more than ten times the size of the lease payments.  Operating cash flow adds further coverage.  If a short‑term shortfall were to arise, the revolving credit facility provides an immediate source of funds, and the firm’s covenant compliance ensures that the facility remains available.  At the same time, the firm limits credit‑risk exposure by keeping cash at top‑tier banks, diversifying its receivable base, monitoring marketplace partners, and using advance‑payment requirements when needed.  This combination of abundant liquid assets, a well‑structured credit line, and disciplined risk‑management practices enables the company to meet its lease obligations while safeguarding overall liquidity.

Because the tax law limits the amount of gambling losses you may claim to **no more than the amount of gambling winnings you actually reported**.  

* In your case you had **$5,400 of gambling winnings** that must be reported in full as income on your return.  
* The Internal Revenue Code (and the guidance in the excerpt) says you can then **itemize gambling losses on Schedule A, but only up to the amount of those winnings**.  
* Therefore the deductible portion of your losses is **$5,400**. The remaining **$300 ($5,700 – $5,400)** is not allowed as a deduction; it simply cannot be used to offset other income or other deductions.

### How this interacts with your reservist expenses

Your reservist‑related expenses are treated under a different set of rules:

| Expense | How it is treated | Where it is reported |

| **Transportation (travel > 100 mi)** – $500 | **Deductible** as an **adjustment to income** (not an itemized deduction) | **Schedule 1, line 8** (or the appropriate line for “unreimbursed employee expenses – reservist”) |
| **Uniform purchase & cleaning** – $250 | **Not deductible** (it is a miscellaneous employee expense that is disallowed) | Not reported; it is simply excluded from the deduction calculation |

So, on your return you would:

1. **Report the full $5,400 of gambling winnings** as income.  
2. **Itemize on Schedule A** a gambling‑loss deduction of **$5,400** (the maximum allowed).  
3. **Enter the $500 reservist travel expense** on Schedule 1 as an adjustment to income.  
4. **Leave the $250 uniform expense off the return** because it is nondeductible.

In short, the tax code caps gambling‑loss deductions at the amount of winnings, which is why you cannot deduct the entire $5,700 loss. Your reservist travel expense is still deductible, but it is taken as an adjustment on Schedule 1, while the uniform cost is disallowed.

**What the international tax changes could do**

* **15 % global minimum tax (Pillar Two).**  
  * The filing notes that many jurisdictions have already enacted Pillar‑Two rules, but for 2024‑2025 the impact on Google was “immaterial.”  
  * The company also warns that as more countries adopt the minimum‑tax regime, “our effective tax rate and cash tax payments could increase in future years.” An increase in cash tax outflows would reduce the pool of cash that could be used for discretionary items such as share repurchases, but the filing does not quantify any current reduction.

* **January 2026 OECD “Side‑by‑Side Safe Harbor.”**  
  * The safe‑harbor provision **exempts U.S. domestic operations of U.S.–parented companies from the global minimum‑tax rules**, although foreign subsidiaries would still be subject to any local minimum‑tax requirements.  
  * Because the bulk of Google’s cash is generated by its U.S. operations, the safe harbor limits the immediate tax‑rate impact of Pillar Two on the cash that is available for repurchases.

**Putting the two together**

1. **Current cash cushion is huge** – $126.8 billion versus a $240 million repurchase need. Even if the global minimum tax raised Google’s cash tax outlays by several hundred million dollars, the company would still have more than $126 billion of liquid resources.  
2. **The safe harbor further shields the U.S. side of the business** from the new 15 % minimum‑tax calculation, meaning the most cash‑generating portion of Google’s earnings is unlikely to see a material increase in tax liability in the near term.  
3. **Future risk** – The filing cautions that as additional jurisdictions adopt the minimum‑tax rules and transitional relief expires, “our effective tax rate and cash tax payments could increase.” If those increases become sizable, they could modestly shrink the cash available for share‑repurchase or other discretionary uses, but the company’s disclosed cash position suggests there is ample headroom to absorb such changes without jeopardizing the $240 million program.

**Bottom line:**  
Based on the information provided, the 15 % global minimum tax and the January 2026 OECD Side‑by‑Side Safe Harbor are not expected to materially constrain Google’s ability to fund its 2025 $240 million share‑repurchase program. The company’s cash balance is orders of magnitude larger than the repurchase amount, and the safe harbor limits the immediate tax impact on the cash‑generating U.S. operations. Only if future international tax liabilities grow substantially could they begin to affect discretionary cash uses, but that risk is described as “potential” and not yet material.

**Potency and metabolic stability of the five AI‑predicted molecules (P1‑P5)**  

* **Overall ranking** – When the five newly synthesised compounds are plotted together with the 160‑molecule training set (Figure 5), the two best‑scoring AI hits, **P1 and P3**, fall in the most favourable quadrant of the potency‑vs‑MLM‑stability scatter plot.  Using the multi‑objective score that sums the rank of IC₅₀ (potency) and the rank of mouse‑liver‑microsome (MLM) stability, **P1 is ranked 1st and P3 2nd out of 165 molecules**.  This means that, despite being 3‑ to 6‑fold less potent than the lead UZH2, they are at least as potent as the majority of the training‑set compounds while showing **much longer metabolic half‑lives (≈5–6 h)** – a several‑fold increase over the best training‑set analogues and far above the 24 min MLM half‑life of UZH2.

* **P2 and P4 (spiro‑morpholine scaffold)** – Both belong to the 29 training‑set molecules that contain the same spiro‑morpholine core.  Within this scaffold‑restricted pool, **P4 ranks 5th and P2 ranks 14th** for the combined potency/MLM metric, i.e. they are above‑average for both properties.  P4 is also one of the most metabolically stable spiro‑morpholine compounds in the set.

* **P5** – This analogue is the weakest of the five; its nanomolar IC₅₀ (≈850 nM) places it at rank 37 in the whole set, reflecting the loss of potency that the authors note.

* **Comparison with the hold‑out set predictions** – In the retrospective hold‑out experiment only **five of the 20 hold‑out molecules were ever predicted**, and they were predicted only a few times (6, 4, 2, 2, 1).  The hold‑out predictions therefore represent a modest hit‑rate and, as the authors point out, the model tended to reproduce the **same spiro scaffold** that dominates the training data, changing mainly the peripheral substituents.

**What Figure 2 tells us about scaffold reliance**  

Figure 2 shows two representative examples of the transformer’s output for molecules that belong to the hold‑out set but were never seen during training.  In both cases the **core spiro scaffold is retained**, while the **substituents are altered** (e.g., methyl, fluoro or chloro groups, or small side‑chain modifications).  This pattern mirrors the quantitative observation that most active training‑set compounds share the spiro scaffold of the lead UZH2.  Consequently, the fine‑tuned transformer learns to **preserve the spiro core** and explore chemical space by decorating it, rather than proposing entirely new scaffolds.

**Take‑away**  

* The five AI‑designed molecules, especially P1 and P3, are **potent and markedly more metabolically stable** than the bulk of the training‑set molecules and far exceed the metabolic profile of the original lead (UZH2).  
* Within the spiro‑morpholine subset, P2 and P4 also outperform the average training‑set members, confirming that the model can improve on existing scaffold‑based chemistry.  
* The scaffold‑preserving transformations illustrated in Figure 2 reveal that the transformer’s optimisation strategy for METTL3 hinges on the **pre‑existing spiro scaffold**, exploiting it as a “fixed backbone” and varying only the surrounding substituents.  This explains both the high frequency of spiro‑based predictions and the limited scaffold diversity among the hold‑out set hits.

A stronger U.S. dollar makes every foreign‑currency amount that Amazon must translate into dollars worth less.  

* **Assets, liabilities and cash equivalents** – The balances of its overseas subsidiaries (including cash and marketable‑securities held in pounds, euros, Canadian dollars, yen, etc.) are converted to U.S. dollars at the period‑end exchange rate. When the dollar appreciates, those foreign‑currency balances translate into a smaller dollar amount, so the reported value of the assets, liabilities and cash equivalents is reduced and can create a material shortfall versus expectations.  

* **Translation adjustments** – The change in the dollar value of those translated items is recorded in “Accumulated other comprehensive income (loss).” A 10 % strengthening of the dollar, for example, would have produced an adverse $180 million (and $136 million a year earlier) impact to that component of equity.  

* **Foreign‑exchange risk** – Because a large share of Amazon’s revenue and operating costs are denominated in non‑dollar currencies (most notably euros), a stronger dollar lowers the dollar‑denominated revenue and expense figures after translation. This can increase the volatility of reported earnings, generate foreign‑currency transaction losses (e.g., the $352 million net foreign‑currency gain for 2025 versus losses in other periods), and reduce the effectiveness of hedging programs, which must offset the adverse translation effect.  

In short, when the U.S. dollar strengthens, Amazon’s foreign‑exchange exposure works against it: foreign‑currency assets, liabilities and cash equivalents translate into fewer dollars, translation adjustments flow to a loss in equity, and the company may record larger foreign‑currency transaction losses that can materially affect its revenue and earnings.

The audit opinion on Microsoft’s internal control over financial reporting does **not** refer to the company’s “zero‑trust end‑to‑end architecture” that is part of its Security Development Lifecycle (SDL).  

Here’s what the two sections say and how they relate (or don’t relate) to each other:

| What the document says | Where it appears in the context |
|------------------------|--------------------------------|
| **Audit opinion on internal control** – The independent accounting firm (Deloitte & Touche) states that Microsoft “maintained, in all material respects, effective internal control over financial reporting” as of June 30 2025, based on the COSO Internal Control – Integrated Framework. The opinion also notes that there have been no material changes to internal control during the quarter ended Jan 25 2026, aside from an ongoing ERP upgrade. | “Opinion on Internal Control over Financial Reporting … In our opinion, the Company maintained, in all material respects, effective internal control …” (multiple paragraphs in the audit opinion). |
| **Security Development Lifecycle (SDL) and zero‑trust architecture** – Microsoft describes its SDL as embedding security and privacy throughout product development and mentions that it “adopts a zero‑trust end‑to‑end architecture.” This is presented as part of the company’s broader Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework, which monitors computing environments, vulnerabilities, and cyber‑threats. | “We integrate security into our computing environments, products, and services through our Security Development Lifecycle (‘SDL’). … through the adoption of zero‑trust end‑to‑end architecture.” (the ERM/SDL paragraph). |
| **Enterprise Risk Management (ERM)** – The ERM program uses COSO guidance for risk management and ISO 31000, and it “supports management in this commitment by facilitating the semiannual risk assessment … aligns them with our strategic mitigation efforts.” | The ERM paragraph that follows the SDL description. |

### Why the audit opinion doesn’t mention the zero‑trust architecture

1. **Scope of the audit** – The PCAOB audit of internal control over financial reporting is limited to controls that affect the **financial reporting process** (e.g., accounting policies, ERP systems, segregation of duties, financial statement preparation, and related disclosures). It does **not** evaluate technical security controls that protect product code, cloud services, or the underlying IT infrastructure unless those controls have a direct, material impact on the accuracy of the financial statements.

2. **Different control domains** –  
   * **Financial‑reporting controls** are judged against the COSO Internal Control – Integrated Framework. The audit looks at things like the design and operating effectiveness of the ERP system, the audit committee’s oversight, management’s assessment, and any material changes to those controls.  
   * **Security controls** (SDL, zero‑trust architecture) belong to the **IT‑security / cyber‑risk** domain. They are part of Microsoft’s ERM program, which the company says “supports management” and “aligns with COSO guidance on Enterprise Risk Management,” but the audit opinion on financial reporting does not require a detailed discussion of those technical controls.

3. **No material linkage identified** – In the excerpts provided, the audit report only mentions an ERP upgrade as a change that could affect internal control. There is no statement that the zero‑trust architecture was examined, found deficient, or praised. The absence of any comment means the auditors either found it **outside the scope** of the financial‑control audit or it had **no material effect** on the financial reporting controls.

### How the two pieces fit together conceptually

- **Risk Management Context** – Microsoft’s ERM framework (which follows COSO guidance) *does* reference the same COSO principles that underlie the internal‑control audit. In that sense, the security architecture is part of the broader risk‑management environment that management says it monitors.  
- **Audit Focus** – The independent auditor’s opinion is a **stand‑alone statement** that, as of the audit date, the company’s internal control over financial reporting was effective. It does not provide an assessment of the SDL or zero‑trust architecture, nor does it say those controls are required for the financial‑reporting opinion.

### Bottom line

- The audit opinion **does not mention** Microsoft’s zero‑trust end‑to‑end architecture at all.  
- The audit’s conclusion about internal control over financial reporting is based on COSO criteria and focuses on financial‑reporting processes (e.g., ERP system, audit committee oversight).  
- The zero‑trust architecture is described in a separate section about Microsoft’s security and ERM practices; it is part of the company’s overall risk‑management strategy but is **not evaluated** in the financial‑control audit.  

So, while both the audit opinion and the SDL description reference COSO‑based frameworks, the audit opinion does not provide any specific commentary on the zero‑trust architecture, and there is no direct connection made between that security design and the auditor’s assessment of internal control over financial reporting.
reference: The risk‑management description says the organization integrates security into its computing environments, products and services through its Security Development Lifecycle and has adopted a zero‑trust end‑to‑end architecture. The independent auditor’s report states that, based on the COSO Internal Control—Integrated Framework, the company maintained, in all material respects, effective internal control over financial reporting as of June 30 2025. The audit opinion does not specifically comment on the zero‑trust architecture; it focuses on the effectiveness of internal financial controls. Both sections demonstrate the use of COSO‑based frameworks—security uses zero‑trust within the SDL, and the financial side received an unqualified audit opinion confirming effective internal controls.

In this car‑dealer example the $2,000 of U.S. currency is well below the $10,000 reporting threshold, and the $9,500 cashier’s check is **not** treated as cash because it is the proceeds of a bank loan.  
Under the “exception for certain bank loans” a cashier’s check (or bank draft, traveler’s check, money order) is excluded from the definition of cash when it is issued as a loan‑proceeds payment. Because the check is excluded, the dealer does **not** have to file Form 8300 for the transaction.

**What you must keep as proof that the cashier’s check is not cash**

The IRS allows you to rely on any of the following to show that the check is loan proceeds:

* a copy of the loan agreement/document showing the loan amount and that the check is being issued to the dealer, **or**  
* a written statement from the bank (or the lien instruction that the bank provided) indicating that the check is being issued as security for the loan, **or**  
* any similar documentation that clearly demonstrates the check is the result of a bank loan.

Retaining one of those items in your records will substantiate the exemption and protect you in case the transaction is later reviewed.

The agreement makes it clear that **getting an MVPD to carry the Tube Media Corp. service is the Affiliate’s responsibility, and it is done by authorizing the MVPD and then using “reasonable efforts” to secure its agreement to retransmit the signal.**  

In practice the steps are:

1. **Authorization** – The Affiliate (the broadcast‑station owner) must give the MVPD permission to carry the Service. The license expressly allows the Affiliate to “authorize, and shall use reasonable efforts to obtain, carriage of the Service’s signal by MVPDs that retransmit digital Broadcast Television signals in the DMA of each Station that transmits the Service.”

2. **Reasonable‑effort outreach** – The Affiliate must actively pursue the MVPD, presenting the Service’s feed (the Primary Feed) and negotiating carriage. This includes providing the MVPD with the necessary technical feed (over‑the‑air, translator, fiber or microwave connections) and any required marketing or promotional materials.

3. **Notification of over‑the‑air launch** – When a broadcast station in the MVPD’s DMA begins transmitting the Service over‑the‑air, the Network must give the Affiliate at least 45 days’ written notice, and the Affiliate must forward that notice to the MVPD. This lets the MVPD know when exclusive over‑the‑air rights take effect and when its carriage may need to be adjusted.

4. **Reporting and compliance** – Once the MVPD agrees to carry the Service, it must (within 30 days after each calendar quarter) provide a certified report of the number of “Digital Cable Subscriber Households” it serves in the relevant DMA. If the MVPD fails to report, the Network and Affiliate will estimate the subscriber count using the formulas set out in Exhibit D (Nielsen/FOCUS data multiplied by national penetration estimates).

5. **Ongoing cooperation** – The Network and Affiliate must cooperate to keep the MVPD’s carriage agreement current, to obtain the required reports, and to address any changes (e.g., a new over‑the‑air station gaining exclusive rights).

So, **the way to get MVPDs to carry the TubeMediaCorp service is to (a) grant them authorization, (b) actively negotiate and secure carriage using reasonable‑effort outreach, (c) keep them informed of broadcast‑station launches, and (d) maintain the reporting and compliance process required by the agreement.**

The Company limits concentration and credit risk in two main ways:

**Cash and cash equivalents**  
* Diversification –* Cash and cash‑equivalent balances are kept with a small number of large, high‑credit‑quality financial institutions.  The Company concentrates deposits with these “big‑bank” counterparties and holds the cash‑equivalents (money‑market funds) in securities that are primarily U.S. government and agency obligations.  
* Investment quality –* Any marketable debt securities it holds are invested in highly‑rated government, agency and investment‑grade corporate issues and are spread across many issuers, so no single counter‑party represents a material share of the cash‑equivalents portfolio.  

**Accounts receivable**  
* Credit monitoring –* The Company continuously evaluates the financial condition of its customers, brand partners and the third‑party online marketplaces that collect payments on its behalf.  It looks at aging, payment terms, geography, historical loss experience and other risk factors each reporting period.  
* Advance‑payment requirements –* When a customer’s credit profile warrants it, the Company may require an advance payment to mitigate the risk of non‑payment.  
* Allowance for credit losses –* It maintains an allowance for estimated credit losses (recorded as a credit‑loss expense in G&A) and adjusts that allowance as conditions change.  
* No single concentration –* The disclosures state that no individual customer accounted for 10 % or more of total accounts‑receivable or revenue in any of the recent years, and the one online marketplace that contributes the largest share still represents only a modest percentage of both receivables and revenue.  

**Result**  
By keeping cash deposits and marketable securities diversified among high‑quality institutions, continuously monitoring the creditworthiness of customers and the online marketplaces that remit funds, and using advance‑payment terms and a credit‑loss allowance, the Company reduces the concentration of credit risk and limits the impact that any single customer or marketplace could have on its financial results.

The Company generates most of its revenue from U.S. and international customers who buy its products on third‑party online marketplaces. It regularly reviews the financial condition of these marketplaces to ensure they can collect funds from customers and remit them to the Company. In addition, the Company has receivables from brand partners and other customers, and it continuously evaluates the financial health of customers and brand partners, sometimes requiring advance payments to mitigate potential credit risks.

**Yes – the IRS may still contact third parties even when you have a duly‑authorized representative.**  

The rules that apply are set out in the “Potential Third‑Party Contacts” section of the IRS’s Taxpayer Bill of Rights:

| What the IRS can do | What you can do |
|----------------------|-----------------|
| **Contact other people** (e.g., a neighbor, bank, employer, employee) if it needs information you haven’t been able to provide or if it must verify information it already has. | **Request a list of everyone the IRS has contacted** about your case. |
| The IRS will only disclose the **minimum information necessary** (usually just your name). | You may make the request **by telephone, in writing, or during a personal interview** with the examiner. |
| The IRS can keep contacting third parties **as long as there is activity in your case** (i.e., while the examination is ongoing). | You can ask for the list **at any time** during the audit; the request does not have to wait until the audit is finished. |

### How to get the list

1. **Call the IRS** (the phone number on any notice you’ve received) and ask for a “list of third‑party contacts” for your examination.  
2. **Write a request** and mail it to the address on the audit notice, stating that you are exercising your right to know who the IRS has spoken with regarding your case.  
3. **Ask for it during a personal interview** if you are meeting the examiner in person. Mention that you want the list as part of your right to confidentiality.

### Why this is allowed even with a representative

- The IRS’s primary point of contact is you **or your authorized representative**, but the law also permits limited outreach to third parties when the information cannot be obtained from you directly.  
- The representative does **not** block the IRS from seeking verification from a bank, employer, neighbor, etc.; it only means the IRS will first try to work through you or your designee.

### Summary

- **Yes**, the IRS can still talk to a neighbor, bank, employer, etc., while an audit is under way, even if you have a representative.  
- They will only share the minimal data required (generally just your name).  
- **You have a right to know** who they have contacted. Request the list by phone, in writing, or at a personal interview.  

If you need further assistance, you may also consult a tax professional or a Low‑Income Taxpayer Clinic, which can help you exercise these rights during the examination.

response:
**1.  How the substantial‑presence test (SPT) works for a taxpayer like Robert Bach**

| Year | Days physically present in the U.S. | Does the SPT‑threshold (≥ 183 days) get met? | Resulting tax status |
|------|--------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------|----------------------|
| **2024** | May 1 – Nov 5 (≈ 188 days) | **Yes** – 188 ≥ 183 | **Resident alien** for the whole 2024 calendar year (dual‑status is not needed because the whole year is covered). |
| **2025** | Returned March 5 as a lawful permanent resident (LPR) | He already was a resident in the *preceding* calendar year (2024).  Under the “Residency during the preceding year” rule, a person who was a resident at any time in the prior year is automatically treated as a resident **as of January 1** of the current year. | **Resident alien for the entire 2025 year**.  The residency‑starting date is therefore **January 1 2025**, even though he did not physically return until March 5. |

*Why the “first‑year choice” does not apply to Robert*  
The first‑year choice is only available when a person **does not** meet either the green‑card test or the SPT in the year of arrival (or the year before) and later meets the SPT.  Robert already satisfied the SPT in 2024, so his residency is automatically carried forward to 2025; no election is required.

*If Robert had **not** met the SPT in 2024*  
- He could have waited until he met the SPT in 2026.  
- By making a **first‑year choice** he could elect to be treated as a resident for part of 2025.  
- To make the election he would have to attach a statement to his 2025 return (see Pub. 519, “First‑Year Choice”) indicating the date he first became present in 2025 and that he is electing resident status for the period from that date to December 31 2025.

**2.  Filing the correct return when the status is known**

| Situation | Form(s) to file | How to indicate dual‑status (if any) |
|-----------|----------------|--------------------------------------|
| Full‑year resident (as in Robert’s actual case) | **Form 1040** (or 1040‑SR) | No special checkbox needed; file the regular resident return. |
| Dual‑status (part‑year resident, part‑year nonresident) | **Form 1040** for the resident portion **plus** a **Form 1040‑NR** used as a “statement” for the nonresident portion. | On the top of each form check the “Other” box and write “Dual Status Return” on the 1040 and “Dual Status Stmt” on the 1040‑NR. Attach the 1040‑NR as a statement showing only the U.S.–source income earned while a nonresident. |
| First‑year choice election | Same as dual‑status (1040 + 1040‑NR) plus a written election statement (usually attached to the return). | The election statement must explain the choice and the residency‑starting date. |

**3.  What to do if the residency classification is later discovered to be wrong**

1. **Determine the correct classification** (resident vs. nonresident) for the year in question.  
2. **Prepare an amended return**:  
   - Use **Form 1040‑X** (Amended U.S. Individual Income Tax Return).  
   - Attach the **corrected 1040** (if the corrected status is resident) **or** the **corrected 1040‑NR** (if the corrected status is nonresident).  
   - If the year becomes a dual‑status year after the correction, attach both the 1040 and the 1040‑NR with the “Dual Status” notations described above.  
   - Include a clear explanation on Form 1040‑X of why the residency status changed (e.g., “After review of days present, the taxpayer meets the substantial‑presence test for 2024 and therefore should be treated as a resident alien for the entire year”).  
3. **File the amendment**:  
   - Send the completed Form 1040‑X and all supporting forms to the address listed in the Form 1040‑X instructions (the address depends on the state of residence).  
   - If you are amending a return that was originally filed electronically, you may also be able to submit the amendment electronically through the IRS e‑file system (if the software you used supports it).  

**4.  Timing and processing of the amendment**

| Rule | Detail |
|------|--------|
| **Statute of limitations** | An amendment must be filed **within 3 years** from the date the original return was filed **or within 2 years** from the date the tax was paid, whichever is later. |
| **IRS processing time** | The IRS typically processes Form 1040‑X in **8‑12 weeks** for most returns; complex dual‑status or first‑year‑choice cases can take **12‑16 weeks** or longer.  The IRS will send a confirmation notice when the amendment is accepted. |
| **Interest and penalties** | If the amendment results in additional tax, interest accrues from the original due date (including extensions) until the tax is paid.  Penalties may apply if the additional tax is not paid promptly. |
| **Refunds** | If the amendment shows that you over‑paid, the IRS will issue a refund (generally by direct deposit if you provided bank information on the 1040‑X).  Refunds are usually issued within 6 weeks after the amendment is accepted. |

**5.  Quick checklist for Robert (or any similar taxpayer) who discovers a mis‑classification**

1. Re‑count days present in the U.S. for the year in question.  
2. Verify whether the SPT (or green‑card test) is met.  
3. Decide the correct filing status (resident, nonresident, or dual‑status).  
4. Complete the appropriate tax return(s):  
   - Full‑year resident → Form 1040.  
   - Full‑year nonresident → Form 1040‑NR.  
   - Dual‑status → Form 1040 + Form 1040‑NR with “Dual Status” notations.  
5. Prepare **Form 1040‑X** with:  
   - Corrected return(s).  
   - Explanation of the change.  
   - Any additional schedules (e.g., Schedule A, Schedule B) that are affected.  
6. Mail (or e‑file) the amendment within the 3‑year window.  
7. Keep copies of all documents and monitor the IRS “Where’s My Amended Return?” tool for status updates.  

**Bottom line:**  
- The substantial‑presence test looks at the number of days physically present in the U.S. during a calendar year; meeting the 183‑day threshold makes you a resident alien for that year, and if you were a resident in the prior year you are automatically treated as a resident from **January 1** of the current year.  
- The first‑year choice is only a fallback election when you *did not* meet the SPT (or green‑card test) in the year of arrival but later do; it lets you retroactively elect resident status for part of the earlier year.  
- If you later discover that you filed the wrong type of return, you correct it with **Form 1040‑X**, attach the proper 1040/1040‑NR (and dual‑status statements if needed), and the IRS will process the amendment within roughly 2–4 months, provided you file within the statutory three‑year window.
reference:
In the example, Robert Bach’s U.S. residency is determined by the substantial presence test. Because he was present in the United States for a sufficient number of days in 2024, he qualified as a resident for that calendar year, and the IRS treats his residency for 2025 as beginning on January 1, 2025. If a taxpayer does not meet the green‑card test or the substantial presence test for a given year but later meets the substantial presence test, the first‑year choice allows the taxpayer to elect to be treated as a resident for part of the earlier year, provided the election requirements are satisfied. 

If the residency determination changes after a return has been filed, the taxpayer must file an amended return. The IRS directs filers to use Form 1040‑X, which can be accessed at IRS.gov/1040X. After filing, the status of the amended return can be checked at IRS.gov/WMAR. The system may take up to three weeks from the filing date for the amended return to appear, and the overall processing time can be as long as sixteen weeks. These steps ensure that the corrected resident or nonresident alien status is reflected in the taxpayer’s final tax liability.

The Document Upload Tool is **only** for responding to eligible IRS notices and letters by securely uploading the documents the IRS has asked for. It isn’t a general portal for submitting new expense claims such as a “car‑modification medical expense.”

If you need to claim that expense (or correct a previously‑filed return), you would have to:

**How the algal‑derived oxygen is used in a photo‑bioelectrochemical system (PBES)**  

1. **Algal photosynthesis in the bioreactor** – Micro‑algae or cyanobacteria absorb light, CO₂ and nutrients and, through photosynthesis, split water. The by‑product of this reaction is molecular oxygen (O₂).  

2. **Transfer of the O₂ to the cathode** – The oxygen that accumulates in the algal culture diffuses (or is pumped) into the cathodic compartment of the PBES.  
   * At the cathode the O₂ acts as the **electron acceptor** for the electrochemical reaction.  
   * It is reduced either directly to water or to reactive oxygen species (ROS) such as H₂O₂·OH, which are powerful oxidants that assist in the degradation of organic pollutants.  
   * The presence of a steady O₂ supply improves the cathodic reaction kinetics, raises the overall cell voltage and therefore the power that can be harvested.  

3. **Resulting benefits** – The algal‑generated O₂ creates a **symbiotic loop**: the algae get CO₂ (or bicarbonate) from the anode side, while the BES supplies O₂ that boosts cathodic reduction and pollutant removal, leading to higher bio‑energy recovery.

---

**How semiconductor photo‑electrodes contribute to pollutant degradation and bio‑energy production**

| Step | Photochemical role of the semiconductor | Effect on pollutant removal / energy generation |
|------|-------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| **Light absorption** | Materials such as TiO₂, WO₃, Fe₂O₃, Co₃(PO₄)₂/Mg(OH)₂ absorb photons and generate electron‑hole pairs. | Provides a pool of **photo‑excited electrons** that can be added to the bio‑generated electron flow. |
| **Electron‑hole separation** | Holes oxidize water or organic contaminants at the photo‑anode; electrons travel through the external circuit to the cathode. | Direct oxidation of recalcitrant pollutants (e.g., dyes, pharmaceuticals) by holes; electrons increase the cathodic current. |
| **Coupling with microbes** | Microbes on the anode oxidize organic substrates, releasing electrons that join the photo‑generated electrons. | **Higher total electron flux** → larger current density and higher power output. |
| **Cathodic reactions** | Photo‑excited electrons arriving at the cathode combine with the O₂ supplied by algae, reducing O₂ to H₂O or ROS, or reduce CO₂ to value‑added products (e.g., H₂). | Accelerated **oxygen reduction** and **hydrogen evolution**, both of which contribute to pollutant mineralisation and bio‑energy capture. |
| **Overall synergy** | The semiconductor acts as a “light‑driven booster” for the microbial electrochemical cell, while the microbes supply organic fuel and maintain a low‑impedance pathway for electrons. | **Improved pollutant degradation rates** (COD removal > 90 %) and **enhanced electricity generation** compared with a purely biological BES. |

---

**Reported power‑density values for the different components / configurations**

| Configuration / study | Reported power density | Units | What the value refers to |
|-----------------------|------------------------|-------|--------------------------|
| **Algal‑assisted PBES (sunlight‑driven algal bioreactor + BES)** | **2.2 W m⁻³** | W m⁻³ | Maximum power density measured after 1 year of continuous operation (Xiao et al. 2012). |
| **General PBES with semiconductor photo‑electrodes (optimal light)** | **24.4 mW m⁻²** | mW m⁻² | Power density achieved under optimal illumination (Yi et al. 2022; Rafieenia et al. 2022). |
| **Diatom‑based BES integrated with photocatalytic/photo‑electric modules** | **20–30 mW m⁻²** | mW m⁻² | Range depending on light intensity and substrate concentration (Vinayak et al. 2021). |
| **Sediment BES with solar‑enhanced bio‑electro‑Fenton (BEF) process** | **44.6 W m⁻³** | W m⁻³ | Peak power density reported for the hybrid sediment‑based system (value cited in the review). |
| **Solar‑driven photo‑bioelectrochemical cell (s‑PBEC) using Co₃(PO₄)₂/Mg(OH)₂ photocatalyst anode** | *Improved* electricity generation (exact figure not given) | – | Demonstrates that adding this photocatalyst raises the cell’s electrical output relative to a non‑photo‑enhanced BES (Rafieenia et al. 2024). |

**Take‑away:**  
- The oxygen produced by algae is funneled to the cathode where it serves as the terminal electron acceptor, enabling efficient reduction reactions that both degrade pollutants and close the electrical circuit.  
- Semiconductor photo‑electrodes harvest light energy, generate extra electrons, and create reactive holes; together with the microbial electron supply they boost both contaminant oxidation (via holes and ROS) and cathodic reduction (via O₂ or CO₂).  
- Reported power densities span from a few tens of milliwatts per square metre for light‑driven PBESs to several watts per cubic metre for long‑term algal‑assisted or sediment‑based configurations, illustrating the scalability of the technology.
reference: The algal bioreactor uses sunlight to run photosynthesis, algae absorb CO2 and nutrients and release oxygen; this photosynthesis‑driven oxygen is then fed to the cathode of the BES where it acts as an electron acceptor and boosts the electrochemical reactions. In the photo‑bioelectrochemical system (PBES) semiconductor photoelectrodes are coupled with anodes and microorganisms act as electrocatalysts, so the photochemical processes together with the oxygen‑rich cathode enable strong pollutant degradation (COD reduction over 90%) and bioelectricity generation. The BES with algal integration recorded a maximum power density of 2.2 W/m³ during one year of operation, while the PBESs under optimal light achieved power densities up to 24.4 mW/m².

Local franchise authorities can influence the company’s assets by imposing or changing taxes, fees, and other assessments that affect the cost of doing business. According to the filing, state and local governments may:

* **Add new or higher taxes/fees** on the company’s services (including franchise, sales, use, and property taxes).  
* **Change the methodology or tax base** used to compute those taxes.  
* **Introduce central‑ or unit‑level assessments** of property taxes or other levies.

These additional or higher tax obligations increase the company’s tax liabilities and cash‑outflows. When tax costs rise, they can reduce earnings and cash available to support assets, potentially leading to:

* **Higher operating expenses** that diminish the recoverable value of long‑lived assets, prompting impairment assessments.  
* **Lower net income**, which can affect the valuation of deferred tax assets and other balance‑sheet items.  
* **Increased overall cost structure**, which may make certain assets less economically viable.

In short, local franchise authorities affect asset impact by altering the tax and fee environment, which can increase tax liabilities, reduce cash flow, and trigger impairments or re‑valuations of the company’s assets.

response:
**Unemployment benefits**

* **General rule** – All unemployment compensation that you receive is taxable income.  
* **Reporting** – The amount shown on Form 1099‑G (box 1) is entered on **Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 7**.  
* **Special cases**  
  * **Private unemployment fund** – Taxable only to the extent the benefits exceed the total contributions you made to the fund; report the taxable portion on **Schedule 1, line 8‑z**.  
  * **Union‑fund benefits** – Included on **Schedule 1, line 8‑z** (or only to the extent they exceed your non‑deductible contributions).  
  * **Guaranteed annual wage** (employer‑guaranteed pay during unemployment) – Treated as wages and reported on **Form 1040 line 1a**.  
  * **Supplemental unemployment benefits** (employer‑financed fund that employees did not contribute to) – Not “unemployment compensation”; they are taxable as wages, subject to withholding and FICA, and are reported on **Form 1040 line 1a**.  
* **Withholding** – You may have 10 % federal tax withheld by filing Form W‑4V. If you do not have tax withheld, you may need to make estimated‑tax payments to avoid a penalty.

---

**Beneficiary taxation on estate or trust income**

1. **You receive a Schedule K‑1 (Form 1041)** from the estate or trust, which shows your share of its income, deductions, and credits.  
2. **Current income that must be distributed** – If the estate/trust is required to distribute all of its current income, you must report **your share of the distributable net income (DNI)** on your return **whether or not you actually received the cash**.  
3. **Current income that is optional to distribute** – If the fiduciary can choose how much to distribute, you must report:  
   * All income that the fiduciary is required to distribute to you (even if not actually paid), **plus**  
   * Any other amounts actually paid or credited to you, up to the total of your share of DNI.  
4. **Treat each item the same way the estate/trust would** – For example:  
   * Dividend income → reported as dividend income.  
   * Tax‑exempt interest → reported as tax‑exempt interest.  
   * Capital gains → reported as capital gains.  
5. **Losses** – Generally not deductible by the beneficiary.  
6. **Excess deductions** – If the estate/trust has deductions that exceed its income in its final year, the excess deductions pass through to you and retain their character (adjustment to AGI, itemized deduction, etc.).  
7. **Grantor trusts** – Income from a grantor trust is taxed to the grantor, not to the beneficiary.  
8. **Business activity** – If the estate or trust is engaged in a U.S. trade or business, you are treated as engaged in the same business for tax purposes.  

In short, unemployment benefits are ordinary taxable income (with a few special rules for private or union funds), and a beneficiary of an estate or trust reports his or her share of the trust’s or estate’s taxable income on the individual return exactly as the entity would have, regardless of whether the cash was actually received.

**Processes that must be put in place before the software can be put into production**

1. **Reporting‑enablement processes** –  
   The Channel Partner (and, separately, each Business Entity that will use the software) must establish the internal procedures that allow the Licensed Software to **send the reports required by the Documentation**.  The agreement states that the Partner must “implement processes that will allow the Licensed Software to successfully report as specified in the Documentation” before any production deployment.    The Partner must create and control the **user‑name/password (Credentials) assignments** for its End Users, and must impose “reasonable limitations on the disclosure of such Credentials.”  This includes setting up the user profiles that the software will use to authenticate End Users to the iPass portal.

3. **Update‑implementation process** –  
   Although not a “pre‑deployment” step, the agreement also requires the Partner to **install all Updates** that iPass releases (especially those that fix errors) before the Partner can rely on Third‑Level Support. **How first‑level technical support ties into those implementation requirements**

- **Responsibility for first‑level support** is placed squarely on the Channel Partner (or the Business Entity on whose behalf the End Users are accessing the service).  The Partner must field all initial support calls from End Users, which will almost always involve **issues with the user profile, credentials, or configuration** that were set up as part of the pre‑deployment processes described above.

- Because the Partner is the one who **creates the user accounts, assigns passwords, and enforces credential‑disclosure limits**, it is also the party that must troubleshoot any problems that arise from those configurations (e.g., a user cannot log in, a profile is missing required attributes, or a reporting configuration is incorrect).
